hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to prominent, dark, vertical or elongated linear structures set against a lighter, often textured background. The activating feature is typically a deep charcoal or black form—such as a vertical fissure, a cast shadow, a dark stalk, a chain, or a biological body—that creates a sharp, high-contrast boundary with the surrounding area. The background is consistently light and desaturated, composed of pale grey, off-white, or beige tones, often featuring fine textures like stone, wood grain, fabric, or fur. The neuron is invariant to whether the dark feature is a positive object (like a slug or chain) or a negative space (like a crack or shadow), as well as the specific material, provided the strong dark-on-light tonal contrast and predominantly vertical orientation are maintained. The activating feature typically spans a significant vertical portion of the frame, occupying approximately 50–90% of the image height and is generally centered or slightly offset horizontally.
